traditions/mekane-yesus/summary: An Ethiopian Lutheran church formed in 1959 from congregations founded by Scandinavian, German and American missions together with indigenous evangelical movements; Presbyterian-origin synods joined in 1974. Persecuted under the Marxist Derg — its general secretary Gudina Tumsa was murdered in 1979 — it grew rapidly to become one of the largest Lutheran churches in the world. It combines Lutheran confession with a strong charismatic and evangelistic piety.
traditions/mekane-yesus/distinctives/0: Holistic ministry: 'serving the whole person' (evangelism and development)
traditions/mekane-yesus/distinctives/1: Charismatic renewal within a Lutheran confession
traditions/mekane-yesus/distinctives/3: Broke fellowship with the Church of Sweden and the ELCA in 2013 over same-sex marriage
traditions/mekane-yesus/distinctives/4: Mekane Yesus Seminary in Addis Ababa
traditions/mekane-yesus/profile/authorit: Scripture as the Word of God, with the ecumenical creeds, the Augsburg Confession and Luther's Small Catechism.
traditions/mekane-yesus/profile/salvatio: Justification by grace alone through faith alone on account of Christ, distinguished carefully as Law and Gospel.
traditions/mekane-yesus/profile/sacramen: Baptism and the Lord's Supper with Lutheran real-presence teaching; healing prayer and deliverance commonly practised.
traditions/mekane-yesus/profile/eschatol: Christ's visible return, the resurrection of the dead and final judgement; amillennial in the confessional tradition.
traditions/mekane-yesus/profile/governan: President and General Assembly with regional synods; Lutheran and Presbyterian elements combined.
traditions/mekane-yesus/profile/worship: Lively worship in Amharic, Oromo and other languages with indigenous music and prayer for healing.
traditions/mekane-yesus/profile/canon: The 66-book Protestant canon; the Apocrypha esteemed for reading but not for doctrine.
traditions/mekane-yesus/status: Active and growing; reported by the Lutheran World Federation as having over ten million members.
traditions/hkbp/summary: The Huria Kristen Batak Protestan, the largest Protestant church in Indonesia, born of the Rhenish Mission among the Toba Batak of North Sumatra, especially through Ludwig Ingwer Nommensen (from 1862). It became autonomous in 1930, received its first Batak ephorus in 1940, and in 1951 adopted its own Confession of Faith — an early example of an Asian church writing its own confession — which allowed it to join the Lutheran World Federation (1952) while retaining a United (Lutheran-Reformed) heritage.
traditions/hkbp/distinctives/0: Rhenish (United) mission heritage with Lutheran confessional identity
traditions/hkbp/distinctives/1: HKBP Confession (1951), addressing local questions such as ancestral practices
traditions/hkbp/distinctives/2: Ephorus as head of the church
traditions/hkbp/distinctives/3: Strong Batak ethnic and cultural identity
traditions/hkbp/profile/authority: Scripture, the ecumenical creeds and the HKBP Confession of Faith (1951, revised 1996).
traditions/hkbp/profile/salvation: Justification by grace alone through faith alone on account of Christ, distinguished carefully as Law and Gospel.
traditions/hkbp/profile/sacraments: Baptism (including infants) and Holy Communion; confirmation of youth.
traditions/hkbp/profile/eschatology: Christ's visible return, the resurrection of the dead and final judgement; amillennial in the confessional tradition.
traditions/hkbp/profile/governance: Ephorus with a synod (Synode Godang) and districts (distrik); church order of 1930 and later revisions.
traditions/hkbp/profile/worship: Liturgical worship in Batak and Indonesian with large choirs and hymnody (Buku Ende).
traditions/hkbp/profile/canon: The 66-book Protestant canon; the Apocrypha esteemed for reading but not for doctrine.
traditions/hkbp/status: Active; several million members in Indonesia and the Batak diaspora.
traditions/laestadian/summary: A conservative Lutheran revival movement begun by Lars Levi Laestadius, pastor in Swedish Lapland, after his awakening in 1844. It spread among Sami, Finns, Swedes and Norwegians and, through emigration, to North America. In the Nordic countries it remains mostly within the national Lutheran churches as lay associations; in North America it formed separate churches (e.g. the Laestadian Lutheran Church and Apostolic Lutheran churches). It has divided into several branches.
traditions/laestadian/distinctives/0: Forgiveness of sins proclaimed by one believer to another 'in Jesus' name and blood'
traditions/laestadian/distinctives/1: Strong sense of the believing congregation as the true church
traditions/laestadian/distinctives/2: Conservative lifestyle (e.g. large families, avoidance of contraception in some branches)
traditions/laestadian/distinctives/3: Summer services (suviseurat) drawing tens of thousands
traditions/laestadian/distinctives/4: Origins among the Sami and in the far north
traditions/laestadian/profile/authority: Scripture and the Lutheran Confessions, with the living word of the believing congregation as the bearer of forgiveness.
traditions/laestadian/profile/salvation: Justification by faith, experienced through hearing and believing the absolution spoken by a fellow believer.
traditions/laestadian/profile/sacraments: Baptism and the Lord's Supper (often received in the national church), with spoken absolution central.
traditions/laestadian/profile/eschatolog: Christ's return and eternal life; strong emphasis on remaining in living faith until the end.
traditions/laestadian/profile/governance: Lay preachers and associations within the national churches; separate congregational churches in North America.
traditions/laestadian/profile/worship: Simple preaching services led by lay preachers, Zion's hymns and the songs of the revival.
traditions/laestadian/profile/canon: The 66-book Protestant canon; the Apocrypha esteemed for reading but not for doctrine.
traditions/laestadian/status: Active in northern Finland, Sweden, Norway and the United States; several branches with differing relations to each other.
traditions/church-of-scotland/summary: Scotland's national Presbyterian church, shaped by the Reformation Parliament of 1560, John Knox and the Scots Confession, and Andrew Melville's Presbyterian polity. After a century of struggle with episcopacy, Presbyterian government was settled in 1690. The Disruption of 1843, over patronage and spiritual independence, split it nearly in half; most of the separated bodies reunited with it in 1929. It is a national church recognised by the state but not controlled by it (Church of Scotland Act 1921).
traditions/church-of-scotland/distinctiv: Presbyterian government by kirk sessions, presbyteries and the General Assembly
Spiritual independence from the state (1921 Act)
traditions/church-of-scotland/profile/au: Scripture as the supreme rule of faith and life, read through Reformed confessions (e.g. Heidelberg Catechism, Second Helvetic Confession, Westminster Standards). The Westminster Confession is its principal subordinate standard, with liberty of opinion on points not entering the substance of the faith.
traditions/church-of-scotland/profile/sa: Salvation by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, grounded in God's sovereign election and expressed in grateful obedience.
Two sacraments, baptism (including infants of believers) and the Lord's Supper, in which believers truly feed on Christ by the Spirit (spiritual real presence).
traditions/church-of-scotland/profile/es: Christ's return, the resurrection and final judgement; amillennial or postmillennial views historically predominant.
traditions/church-of-scotland/profile/go: Presbyterian: elders and ministers in courts of kirk session, presbytery and General Assembly, with an annually chosen Moderator.
traditions/church-of-scotland/profile/wo: Reformed worship centred on preaching; metrical psalms, the Church Hymnary; Communion seasons historically infrequent.
traditions/church-of-scotland/status: Active; membership has fallen sharply to under 300,000 by the 2020s.
traditions/dutch-reformed-pkn/name: Dutch Reformed Church (NHK) and Protestant Church in the Netherlands (PKN)
traditions/dutch-reformed-pkn/summary: The Reformed public church of the Netherlands, organised by the exiles' Synod of Emden (1571) and confirmed in its Calvinist orthodoxy by the Synod of Dort (1618–19). Reorganised in 1816 as the Nederlandse Hervormde Kerk, it suffered secessions in 1834 (Afscheiding) and 1886 (Doleantie, led by Abraham Kuyper), which produced the Gereformeerde Kerken. In 2004 the Hervormde Kerk, the Gereformeerde Kerken and the Evangelical-Lutheran Church merged as the Protestant Church in the Netherlands (PKN); dissenting congregations formed the Restored Reformed Church.
traditions/dutch-reformed-pkn/distinctiv: Three Forms of Unity (Belgic Confession, Heidelberg Catechism, Canons of Dort)
Secessions of 1834 and 1886 and the 2004 merger
Neo-Calvinism of Abraham Kuyper (in the Gereformeerde line)
Mother church of Reformed churches in South Africa, Indonesia and North America
traditions/dutch-reformed-pkn/profile/au: Scripture as the supreme rule of faith and life, read through Reformed confessions (e.g. Heidelberg Catechism, Second Helvetic Confession, Westminster Standards). The PKN's church order also includes the Lutheran confessions and the Barmen Declaration.
traditions/dutch-reformed-pkn/profile/sa: Salvation by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, grounded in God's sovereign election and expressed in grateful obedience.
Two sacraments, baptism (including infants of believers) and the Lord's Supper, in which believers truly feed on Christ by the Spirit (spiritual real presence).
traditions/dutch-reformed-pkn/profile/es: Christ's return, the resurrection and final judgement; amillennial or postmillennial views historically predominant.
traditions/dutch-reformed-pkn/profile/go: Presbyterian-synodal: consistories, classes and a General Synod.
traditions/dutch-reformed-pkn/profile/wo: Reformed worship with Genevan psalms and the Liedboek; a strong orthodox 'Bible Belt' wing alongside liberal congregations.
traditions/dutch-reformed-pkn/status: Active as the PKN, the largest Protestant church in the Netherlands, though declining.
traditions/reformed-church-in-hungary/su: The Calvinist church of Hungarian speakers, consolidated when the Synod of Debrecen (1567) adopted the Second Helvetic Confession and the Heidelberg Catechism. It flourished in Transylvania and eastern Hungary under Ottoman and Transylvanian rule, survived Habsburg Counter-Reformation pressure, and today also has sister churches among Hungarian minorities in Romania, Slovakia, Ukraine and Serbia.
traditions/reformed-church-in-hungary/di: Second Helvetic Confession and Heidelberg Catechism
Historic colleges at Debrecen and Sárospatak
Strong link between Reformed faith and Hungarian identity
traditions/reformed-church-in-hungary/pr: Scripture as the supreme rule of faith and life, read through Reformed confessions (e.g. Heidelberg Catechism, Second Helvetic Confession, Westminster Standards).
Salvation by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, grounded in God's sovereign election and expressed in grateful obedience.
Two sacraments, baptism (including infants of believers) and the Lord's Supper, in which believers truly feed on Christ by the Spirit (spiritual real presence).
Christ's return, the resurrection and final judgement; amillennial or postmillennial views historically predominant.
Presbyterian-synodal with bishops presiding over church districts alongside lay chief curators.
Reformed worship with Genevan psalms in Hungarian and preaching; churches without images.
traditions/reformed-church-in-hungary/st: Active; the second-largest church in Hungary.
traditions/christian-reformed-church/nam: Christian Reformed Church in North America
traditions/christian-reformed-church/sum: A church of Dutch immigrant origin founded in west Michigan in 1857 by congregations that left the Reformed Protestant Dutch Church (today's Reformed Church in America). Shaped by the Seceder tradition and by Abraham Kuyper's neo-Calvinism, it built Calvin University and Seminary and a strong Christian school movement. It opened all offices to women in 1995 (by local option); in 2022 its synod declared that its confessions exclude same-sex sexual relationships, leading some congregations to leave.
traditions/christian-reformed-church/dis: Kuyperian vision of Christ's lordship over all of life
Christian day schools and Calvin University
Dutch-Canadian and Dutch-American heritage now becoming multi-ethnic
traditions/christian-reformed-church/pro: Scripture as the supreme rule of faith and life, read through Reformed confessions (e.g. Heidelberg Catechism, Second Helvetic Confession, Westminster Standards). Officers subscribe to the Three Forms of Unity.
Salvation by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, grounded in God's sovereign election and expressed in grateful obedience.
Two sacraments, baptism (including infants of believers) and the Lord's Supper, in which believers truly feed on Christ by the Spirit (spiritual real presence).
Christ's return, the resurrection and final judgement; amillennial or postmillennial views historically predominant.
Presbyterian: councils, classes and an annual synod.
Reformed worship with psalms and hymns (Psalter Hymnal; Lift Up Your Hearts).
traditions/christian-reformed-church/sta: Active in the United States and Canada; roughly 200,000 members.
